title: Shadows of the Living
subtitle: Metallic sheen, rippling water, and shadows that peer back from within the dim reflection.

trails.title: The Weaving of Shadows, Volume III
trails.description: Rust fills the air, and an exiled bird has found a branch to rest upon.

trails.title: Typewriter Record #P5
trails.description: A woman's documentation of a blind society.

content.text:
... 

Even though they refuse to discuss the outside world, spending even a few days inside the prison makes clear that the reason they are here is precisely what they avoid speaking about.

Ushuaia is a cold town on the tip of Argentina's southernmost territory. The polar night, the frozen sea, the proximity to Antarctica, the endless winter—it all makes the place seem buried by time and forgotten. It possesses all the necessary qualities of a prison, making it an ideal place to send arcanist suspects diagnosed with mental illness, a place to be forgotten.

Setting aside the true definition of madness and their status as prisoners, what I see in this prison are former poets, writers, and social activists. In their era, some spoke of poetry—then disappeared from society for owning a book by Jean-Paul Sartre. Some incited grassroots rebellion against hierarchical structures—only to be exiled. They were repeatedly questioned, "Why do you read these books? Why do you write these poems?" They were branded "thought organizers" and eventually sent here to partake in an experiment conducted under the names of Foucault and psychoanalysis. It is nearly impossible to determine whether their "madness" was defined by society because they resisted order, or if it was induced through relentless electric shocks and torture. Or perhaps all of these reasons are one and the same. This reason is often avoided, sanitized, or ignored—because deep down, we all know how deeply it is woven into the fabric of all our lives.

...

At first, they said nothing, but this very act of deliberate avoidance was what truly conveyed their grief and fear.

items.text: Shadows of the Living
The Researcher awakens in her dune cave, which felt to her as hollow as a tomb. It was a little before dawn.
Stacks of tapes had eaten up her living space, climbing up again and again, each of these spinning reels speaking of stories about that cottage with a blue roof.

She heard the voice of the Murdered Donkey Driver behind her: "I hear them all, the laughter and voices of generations past. Like dry leaves caught in the cracks of old walls, rustling only when the wind blows through. I wouldn't set foot in that house if I were you."
The Door-Side Beggar spoke too: "I sleep on the porch every night. Each morning, a dim light glows through the window. But no one ever leaves through that door ... and no one has ever entered."
Then the Bank Clerk's voice: "It's the story of the 'alter ego.' That house must've been filled with debts no one would return to claim."
The sick old lady, struggling in her bed, whispered: "The house remembers those days, when people vanished in the darkness of night and children were stolen by the storms."
The Paracausality Researcher had heard enough and drifted back to sleep again. There was only the rattling of the Die of Babylon echoing in her hollow cave.
Gallery of Bewilderment
In a deteriorating activity hall, thousands of floating slips of paper form a blurred, colossal face. It is hard to imagine how the prisoners managed to transform this place into what it is now.

items.speaker: García
items.text: I've always wanted to use the element of fantasy to better establish our theme. And I was right.

items.speaker: García
items.text: Now the stage is captivating, the timing is perfect, and the audience is ideally placed.

items.speaker: García
items.text: Only one imperfect element remains in the scene—the creator, who hasn't stepped away from his creation.

items.speaker: García
items.text: No, there's another thing.
García, the curator of the exhibition, stands beneath his work, deep in thought, agonizing over every minute imperfection.
His fellow poets whisper to one another.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: Can you even tell any difference between today's setup and yesterday's?

items.speaker: La Sociedad Member I
items.text: Seriously, Roberta? That's a rude question!

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: Well, what's the difference, then?

items.speaker: La Sociedad Member I
items.text: Well, I can't see one either. But you should never judge art by how much it changes in a day! It's a creative process.

items.speaker: La Sociedad Member I
items.text: We might be standing at the edge of the world, but art has no boundaries! We have to show him our support.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: Easy for you to say. He's been tinkering and tweaking for over three months.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: Even if the Idealist himself entrusted him with this exhibition, he can still be wrong sometimes. This gallery is turning into a dump!
I'm seeing ghosts, all with the same faces, García. All too many. It's easy to get lost in them.
Having navigated through the labyrinth, the Idealist—the leader of La Sociedad—arrives at the exhibit's entrance, accompanied by several new faces and the jailer.

items.speaker: García
items.text: Idealist! You're back. Are these new recruits for La Sociedad? You must have had a very successful day!

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: It is good to see you, García. How has your vision progressed today?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: First a salon, and now an art gallery? Is this really a prison?
Her shock is evident on her face, but her words are ignored as García begins to vent his frustrations.

items.speaker: García
items.text: As you can see, I've strived to push the element of fantasy in my work so that it might reach perfection.

items.speaker: García
items.text: But why doesn't it look like what I imagined?

items.speaker: García
items.text: It's like I'm trying to work on a shadow—some shapeless thing that morphs and shifts by the hour. Idealist, am I losing it again? I took my medicine as instructed.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: It was never the pills that blinded you, my dear García.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: You mustn't let tedious routine stifle what's truly alive. Remember, like those old poems, your exhibition must have a timeless rhythm that's never lost to the changing of minds.
García holds out his hands as if grasping something fleeting but fails to hold onto it.

items.speaker: García
items.text: Sorry, maybe I'm just not getting it.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Look up! There's your answer. Though the sun rises the same way every day, the multitudes of shadows it casts are ever-changing.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Isn't that the only constant in life—change?

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: We foolishly pursue stability and constancy, but our very world denies it. Take a step back—take several—and see the truth for yourself, lest you too become lost among the shifting shadows.

items.speaker: García
items.text: I get it now! It's the changing light that makes the exhibits seem different from what I expected.

items.speaker: García
items.text: I shouldn't waste my time on freezing things in one perfect moment. Instead, I need to embrace change as it comes.

items.speaker: García
items.text: I don't know how to thank you! I won't let you down. I must complete this exhibition.

items.speaker: García
items.text: Complete my "alter ego."
The choice of word widens the writer's eyes.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Did you say "alter ego"?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And he called you García. Is that your name?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: García, where did you learn about this "alter ego"? Do you happen to write under the name—
But the curator has already returned to his work, uninterested or oblivious to his visitors.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Please, Recoleta! Give our artist some space. Can't you see? He's already returned to his own time and space. He can't hear a thing you say.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: He's right. García is deep in his own head now. He won't hear a thing until he's done with whatever he has to do.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: Even if the floor were to collapse out under us, I think he would be left standing in the air without even noticing.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Ah. Pardon me then.
She takes a step back out of respect.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text:
Alright. My dear guests! Please forgive my late introduction. Welcome to the 
Gallery of Bewilderment.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Thank you for inviting me here, Mr. Idealist.
The Foundation's investigators have been carefully observing each prisoner's movements since they arrived. But unfortunately, there is no sign of Ms. Dores.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: I imagine you're curious about what we do here, in the heart of La Sociedad de Poetas de las Américas.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: We're putting together a magazine—a collection of poems from Comala, our very own Casa de las Américas.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Casa de las Américas?!
The Idealist nods with a smile.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Exactly. Named after its great predecessor! You're a fine mind indeed! At this very moment, all our companions are working on it.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: García's exhibition, "Alter Ego," is centered around the birth of this magazine.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: And here, you can see the signatures from all the poets involved, along with a few words they've written for it.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Reading it is like looking into the soul of our society.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: All these signatures ...
Sonetto steps forward to examine the perplexing "artwork." In the dim lighting, the enormous face appears to be looming watchfully over the entire room.
A floating slip of paper catches her attention.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Timekeeper, here! It's Dr. Dores's pseudonym—Urd!

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Then she was here.
Sonetto pockets the slip of paper dutifully.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Precisely. She used to be one of us, and still is, if I may correct myself.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: You can ask around here. Maybe some of our members know where she went.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Don't we all miss the familiar faces of old friends? I'm sure they'll do everything they can to help you find yours.
As he finishes speaking, several enthusiastic prisoners come forward to greet the Idealist.

items.speaker: La Sociedad Member II
items.text: Mr. Idealist, I've finished my short story. It's called "Weightlessness." It drifts around the subject like a sheep floating in space! The readers can start anywhere in the story or read it in any order they like!

items.speaker: La Sociedad Member III
items.text: And please take a look at my piece, "Off Limits!" Every word that has been forbidden is either erased or replaced with symbols. It's a one-of-a-kind jarring experience!

items.speaker: La Sociedad Member IV
items.text: And I've finished a new paragraph! Just wrote it today.
A prisoner, wrapped in several meters of manuscript paper, like a strange sort of mummy, squeezes into the crowd.

items.speaker: La Sociedad Member IV
items.text: Oh! New faces! Welcome!
Without any warning, he calmly tears the manuscript to shreds.
The fluttering fragments fall like trailing sparks from a fireworks show.
The abrupt "welcome ceremony" leaves the newcomers stunned, while the "natives" share knowing smiles.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Idealist! Did he just ...?

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: This is the writer for the prologue of our magazine.
The leader of La Sociedad, either misunderstanding or evading the question, responds with enthusiasm.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: The prologue consists of a two-thousand-line poem and an introduction that is written in 86 languages to avoid misinterpretation. It represents every second we spend here.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Naturally, the arrival of new members disrupts its structure, and so we must begin again from scratch.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: So he just tore it all up like that because he thought we were joining?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: With all due respect, isn't this a little excessive? Heaven knows I'm not one to judge. I've torn up plenty of writing for my novel.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Please pay it no mind. It may not be an easy task, but he's doing his part.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Destruction is hard, but more necessary than you think. Without it, we'd all be stuck in a still and stagnant pond, with all the smells that entail.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: This all sounds very complicated. When will your magazine be finished then?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Forgive me, but I'm not sure what a floating sheep, a jarring reading experience, and all this constant rewriting are meant to express.
The jailer, having remained silent, takes a deep breath and interrupts.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: As I've said, Comala is unlike any other prison.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Ms. Jailer, do you mean ...

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: This place also serves as a research center. And the prisoners here, for all they claim, are not just "poets."

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: They are arcanist criminals, and each one of them has been diagnosed as mentally ill.
The leader of La Sociedad remains composed, like an island in a rough sea,
leaving the onlookers to question whether he is entirely mad or the sanest of them all.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: You're quite right, Jailer. But let's not forget that mental illness is merely a deviation from the norm. And who decides the norm? You? The Physician? Or the ones outside these walls?

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: We've been exiled here by the standards of our time, deprived of our roles in the outside world. So please, as we agreed before, I ask you not to interfere with the affairs of La Sociedad!

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: These people are visitors, not your new recruits.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: But should we not hear their thoughts first?
The Idealist turns toward the visitors with an urgent plea.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: My friends! No one escapes the Eye of Power. We must resist. Stand with us. Pick up your pen and take poetry as your shield before it is too late!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Idealist, I admire your fight. But I came here with a different goal.
The leader of La Sociedad, caught in his fervor, ignores her words and carries on.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: "We're the last true owners of an old legend, words now only remembered as myth."

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: We must stay on the path of literature until I find that transcendental solution ...

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: To invent an idiom that is generic, all-encompassing, yet precise. My poem will be written in this language, leaving no room for doubt or misinterpretation!

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: How blessed is a man with infallible memory! He holds the finer details of each object within him, more vivid than anyone else. In the end, he'll have all the answers, if time allows him!
A dream-like expression crosses his face. It briefly seems as if he has become an entirely different person. But his vision is soon interrupted.

items.speaker: La Sociedad Member IV
items.text: Sweet tank! Sister ... howls! Hermaphrodite—Tango ...!

items.speaker: La Sociedad Member IV
items.text: They put the whole city ... in the nuthouse!

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Timekeeper, look over there!

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Isn't that the prologue writer?!

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: There's something off about him. Please, Timekeeper, stay away from him!

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: What's happening?

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: Idealist! Pablo is having another episode!

items.speaker: La Sociedad Member IV
items.text: Multiples of ... us! You make reality sick!
A flash of arcane energy flares up, and the jailer steps into the crowd reactively.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I could use your help, ladies!
The frenzied prisoner is subdued. He lies convulsing in the center of the exhibit hall.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: Poor soul. I'll bring him to bed.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: Well done, ladies. Aren't you full of surprises!

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: What was all that?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: It seems he had a mental breakdown and lost control of his arcane skill. It appears that every line he recited carried unbridled power.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Usually, only specific lines can channel arcane energy. You can't just force the power into words or craft a poem to serve your purpose.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Pablo must have a rare gift for identifying empowered lines. When he recited them all aloud, they overwhelmed him.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: That's right. He's a genius who rides the tides of emotion, just like Arthur Rimbaud.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: We always keep a close eye on him to make sure he doesn't recite anything while reading or writing.
Roberta trades glances between the tense jailer and her visitors.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: But, sometimes, things slip through.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: You must understand how difficult it is for a poet to never taste the words on his own lips.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: So, then this isn't the first time. And you're all fully aware of it.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Do I understand you right? Did you just admit that you've been hiding an inmate with a dangerous condition from us?

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: According to the Safety Regulations for the Panopticon of Comala, he must be sent to the Physician for immediate treatment.
The jailer's command causes a dramatic shift in the room.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: No, no! Wait, we can explain!

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: He's doing fine! We know how to help him. This was just an accident. We-We got distracted by the new members.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: We won't be handing him over to the Physician.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: No true writer would allow their mind—the most sacred palace of their thoughts—to be opened up to that cold-hearted, ignorant butcher. Even one who believes their inspiration flows from a source beyond the mere substance of a brain would refuse it!
The jailer furrows her brows and pulls out her weapon. The air tightens into an invisible thread.
